slides.title: Section 01 · Big idea
slides.html:
01Up next

The central question

slides.title: Why calculus begins with an instant
slides.html:
Conceptual FrameStart with the question

Calculus is the language of change — including change at a single moment.

Big Idea

How can we describe what is happening at an instant when change usually takes time?

Average rate of change measures change across an interval. Instantaneous rate of change asks what happens at one input value — and that requires limits.

slides.title: Two types of rate — notation
slides.html:
Knowledge PointDistinguish the two rates

Interval language vs. instant language.

Definition · Average rate of change

On \([a,b]\), for a quantity \(f\):

\[\text{Average rate} = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\]

This is the slope of a secant line on the graph of \(f\).

Definition · Instantaneous rate of change (preview)

At \(x=c\), we examine shorter and shorter intervals and take a limit:

\[\text{Instantaneous rate at }c = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h}\]

slides.title: Section 02 · Average rate
slides.html:
02Up next

Average rate of change

slides.title: Position function example
slides.html:
Worked ExampleCompute an average rate

Always identify the interval endpoints first.

A particle has position \(s(t)=t^2+1\) (meters), with \(t\) in seconds.

Key Point · Interval [2, 3]
\[\frac{s(3)-s(2)}{3-2}=\frac{(9+1)-(4+1)}{1}=\frac{10-5}{1}=5\ \text{m/s}\]

Interpretation: on average, the particle moved 5 meters per second from \(t=2\) to \(t=3\).

slides.title: Shorter intervals — approaching an instant
slides.html:
Knowledge PointShrink the interval

Same formula — smaller \(\Delta t\).

From \(t=2\) to \(t=2+h\):

\[\frac{s(2+h)-s(2)}{h}=\frac{(2+h)^2+1-5}{h}=4+h\]
\(h\)IntervalAverage rate \(4+h\)
1[2,3]5
0.5[2,2.5]4.5
0.1[2,2.1]4.1
0.01[2,2.01]4.01
AP Checkpoint
As \(h\to 0\), the average rate approaches 4. That limiting value is the instantaneous rate at \(t=2\).

slides.title: Section 03 · Secant → tangent
slides.html:
03Up next

Secant lines approach a tangent

slides.title: Visual: secant slopes converge
slides.html:
Graphical SkillConnect algebra to the picture

Each secant uses two points; the tangent uses one point and a limiting direction.

Key Point · Geometric meaning
  • Secant slope = average rate on \([2,2+h]\)
  • Tangent slope = instantaneous rate at \(t=2\)
  • When the limit exists, secant slopes approach the tangent slope.

slides.title: Section 04 · Difference quotient
slides.html:
04Up next

Difference quotient

slides.title: Full algebra: simplify before taking the limit
slides.html:
Worked ExampleShow every step

Expand, combine like terms, cancel \(h\).

Simplify \(\displaystyle\frac{s(2+h)-s(2)}{h}\) for \(s(t)=t^2+1\).

\[\begin{aligned}\frac{s(2+h)-s(2)}{h}&=\frac{(2+h)^2+1-(2^2+1)}{h}\\&=\frac{4+4h+h^2+1-5}{h}\\&=\frac{4h+h^2}{h}=4+h\quad (h\neq 0)\end{aligned}\]
\[\lim_{h\to 0}(4+h)=4\]
AP Checkpoint
After simplification, the limit is visible. Without canceling \(h\), the expression is undefined at \(h=0\) — but the limit can still exist.

slides.title: Section 05 · Context graphs
slides.html:
05Up next

Real contexts on graphs

slides.title: Mr. Brust's trip — read the distance graph
slides.html:
ApplicationPacket problem 1.1

Turn around → graph is not monotone; secant slope = average rate.

  1. (a) Average speed whole trip: \(\dfrac{D(8)-D(0)}{8-0}\).
  2. (b) Average rate on \([2,6]\): slope of secant from \(t=2\) to \(t=6\).
  3. (c) Shorter interval \([2,3]\) gives a better estimate of the rate near \(t=2\).
  4. (d) Estimate instantaneous rate at \(t=2\) using \(\dfrac{D(2.1)-D(1.9)}{0.2}\) (tiny interval).

slides.title: Social-media views — tangent interpretation
slides.html:
ApplicationEstimate from a curve

Views per week ≈ slope of tangent at that week.

Channel views \(v(w)\) vs. weeks \(w\). At \(w=10\):

\[\text{Estimate} \approx \frac{v(10.1)-v(9.9)}{0.2}\]
Common Mistake
Do not confuse average rate on an interval with instantaneous rate at a point. The notation \(\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{v(10+h)-v(10)}{h}\) describes the latter.

slides.title: Section 06 · AP practice
slides.html:
06Up next

AP-style practice

slides.title: Question: interpret a difference quotient
slides.html:
Strategy

A difference quotient over \([0,50]\) always describes an average rate on that interval.

Question PracticeTry it first

Work on paper, then check your reasoning.

Buffalo population \(b(t)\), \(t\) = years since 1800. What does \(\dfrac{b(50)-b(0)}{50-0}\) represent?

Choose your answer

slides.title: Answer: buffalo population
slides.html:
Answer ReviewCheck and correct

Compare your work with the model solution.

Correct Answer: B

✦
Your turnReveal only after you've written a full solution.

Solution:

\[\frac{b(50)-b(0)}{50-0}=\text{average rate of change on }[0,50]\]

Years 1800–1850: average change in population per year.

slides.title: Question: instantaneous rate setup
slides.html:
Strategy

Instantaneous rate requires a limit as the interval length goes to 0.

Question PracticeTry it first

Work on paper, then check your reasoning.

For \(s(t)=t^2+1\), which expression represents the instantaneous rate at \(t=2\)?

Choose your answer

slides.title: Answer: instantaneous setup
slides.html:
Answer ReviewCheck and correct

Compare your work with the model solution.

Correct Answer: B

✦
Your turnReveal only after you've written a full solution.

Solution:

Only choice B uses the limit definition of instantaneous rate at \(t=2\).

Lesson outline

Unit 1 · 1.2

Defining limits & limit notation

7 sections · full AP-style progression.

slides.title: Section 01 · What is a limit?
slides.html:
01Up next

What a limit means

slides.title: Informal definition
slides.html:
Knowledge PointApproach, not necessarily equal

A limit describes behavior near a point.

Definition · Limit at a point (informal)
\[\lim_{x\to c} f(x)=L\]

means: as \(x\) gets arbitrarily close to \(c\) (but not necessarily equal to \(c\)), the values \(f(x)\) get arbitrarily close to \(L\).

Key Point · Read it aloud

“The limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) approaches \(c\) is \(L\).”

The arrow \(x\to c\) always refers to the input variable.

slides.title: Formal precision (optional)
slides.html:
Extensionε–δ definition

AP may reference this for rigor; focus on the idea first.

Definition · Limit (precise)
\[\forall \varepsilon>0,\ \exists \delta>0:\ 0<|x-c|<\delta \Rightarrow |f(x)-L|<\varepsilon\]

For every tolerance \(\varepsilon\) on outputs, we can find a distance \(\delta\) on inputs that forces \(f(x)\) within \(\varepsilon\) of \(L\).

slides.title: Section 02 · Notation reference
slides.html:
02Up next

Limit notation cheat sheet

slides.title: Notation you must read fluently
slides.html:
ReferenceSymbols → meaning

Say the limit before computing.

SymbolMeaning
\(\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)=5\)As \(x\to 3\), outputs approach 5
\(\lim_{x\to 3^-} f(x)\)Approach from the left (\(x<3\))
\(\lim_{x\to 3^+} f(x)\)Approach from the right (\(x>3\))
\(f(3)\)Actual function value at \(x=3\) (may differ from the limit)
Common Mistake
A limit statement never guarantees \(f(c)=L\). Always check the graph for a filled dot vs. open circle.

slides.title: Section 03 · Value vs limit
slides.html:
03Up next

Function value vs limit

slides.title: Piecewise example — limit exists but value differs
slides.html:
Worked ExampleCompare \(\lim\) and \(f(c)\)

Simplify on both sides of the hole.

\(f(x)=x+2\) for \(x\neq 3\), and \(f(3)=10\).

\[\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)=\lim_{x\to 3}(x+2)=5,\qquad f(3)=10\]
Key Point · When can they differ?
  • Removable hole: open circle at \((c,L)\), filled dot elsewhere
  • Undefined at \(c\) but limit still exists

slides.title: Section 04 · Graph practice
slides.html:
04Up next

Limits from the packet graph

slides.title: Packet 1.2 — read limits from the graph
slides.html:
Graphical SkillLeft, right, then two-sided

Use the same graph for all items.

  1. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 1} f(x)\) — approach from both sides
  2. \(f(-3)\) — function value, not a limit
  3. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2} f(x)\) — check left vs. right
  4. \(f(2)\) vs. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2} f(x)\) — may differ

slides.title: Interpretation in words
slides.html:
ApplicationTranslate notation

AP free-response often asks for verbal interpretation.

Definition · Verbal form

\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 7} f(x)=10\) means:

As \(x\) approaches 7, the values of \(f(x)\) approach 10.

AP Checkpoint
True or false? \(f(1)=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 1} f(x)\) in all cases. False. Counterexample: any removable discontinuity.

slides.title: Section 05 · AP practice
slides.html:
05Up next

AP-style multiple choice

slides.title: Question: best interpretation
slides.html:
Strategy

Match input approach (\(x\to 4\)) with output approach (\(\to 8\)).

Question PracticeTry it first

Work on paper, then check your reasoning.

Which is the best interpretation of \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 4} f(x)=8\)?

Choose your answer

slides.title: Answer: interpretation
slides.html:

Correct Answer: C

slides.title: Question: limit at x = −1
slides.html:
Strategy

Read the arrow on the input: \(x\to -1\).

Question PracticeTry it first

Work on paper, then check your reasoning.

Which is the best interpretation of \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to -1} f(x)=2\)?

Choose your answer

slides.title: Answer: limit at −1
slides.html:
Answer ReviewCheck and correct

Compare your work with the model solution.

Correct Answer: D

✦
Your turnReveal only after you've written a full solution.

Solution:

Input approaches \(-1\); outputs approach 2.

slides.title: Question: f(1) vs limit
slides.html:
Strategy

A limit can exist even when the function value differs.

Question PracticeTry it first

Work on paper, then check your reasoning.

On a graph, \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 1} f(x)=3\) but \(f(1)=5\). Which is true?

Choose your answer

slides.title: Answer: f(1) vs limit
slides.html:
Answer ReviewCheck and correct

Compare your work with the model solution.

Correct Answer: C

✦
Your turnReveal only after you've written a full solution.

Solution:

Limit 3, value 5 — removable-type mismatch.

Estimating limits from graphs

7 sections · full AP-style progression.

slides.title: Section 01 · One-sided limits
slides.html:
01Up next

One-sided limits

slides.title: Definition: approach from one side
slides.html:
Knowledge PointLeft vs right

Superscript − and + tell you which direction.

Definition · One-sided limits
\[\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x)=L \quad\text{(from the left)},\qquad \lim_{x\to c^+} f(x)=M \quad\text{(from the right)}\]

A one-sided limit is the value \(f(x)\) approaches as \(x\) nears \(c\) from one side only.

slides.title: Two-sided limit exists only when sides agree
slides.html:
Knowledge PointCombine one-sided limits

Different sides → DNE.

Definition · Two-sided limit
\[\lim_{x\to c} f(x)=L \iff \lim_{x\to c^-} f(x)=\lim_{x\to c^+} f(x)=L\]
AP Checkpoint
If left and right limits differ, the two-sided limit does not exist (even if \(f(c)\) is defined).

slides.title: Section 02 · Piecewise graph
slides.html:
02Up next

Classic piecewise graph

slides.title: Read limits at x = 2
slides.html:
Worked ExampleFollow the graph checklist

Open circle = limit; filled dot = function value.

\[\lim_{x\to 2^-} f(x)=3,\quad \lim_{x\to 2^+} f(x)=3,\quad \lim_{x\to 2} f(x)=3,\quad f(2)=1.5\]
Common Mistake
\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2} f(x)\neq f(2)\) — so \(f\) is not continuous at \(x=2\).

slides.title: Section 03 · Packet graphs
slides.html:
03Up next

Packet 1.3 exercises

slides.title: Packet 1.3 — one-sided limits from graphs
slides.html:
ApplicationPacket examples 1–3

Work each limit from the graph before revealing solutions.

  1. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3^-} f(x)=-1\), \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3^+} f(x)=2\) → \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)\) DNE
  2. At \(x=-2\): compare left and right limits
  3. Sketch \(g\) with \(g(3)=-1\), \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3} g(x)=4\), increasing on \((-2,3)\)

slides.title: Graph reading checklist
slides.html:
ReferenceFour questions every time

Use this on every AP graph problem.

Key Point · Graph checklist
  1. What does the graph approach from the left?
  2. What does the graph approach from the right?
  3. Are those values equal?
  4. Where is the filled dot (actual function value)?

slides.title: Section 04 · Sketching
slides.html:
04Up next

Sketching with constraints

slides.title: Design a graph satisfying all conditions
slides.html:
Worked ExampleOpen vs closed dots

Constraints on value, limit, and monotonicity.

Sketch \(g\) such that:

  • \(g(3)=-1\) (filled dot at \((3,-1)\))
  • \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3} g(x)=4\) (open circle at \((3,4)\))
  • \(g\) increasing on \((-2,3)\)
AP Checkpoint
Increasing on \((-2,3)\) means as \(x\) increases toward 3, \(g(x)\) increases — the graph rises toward the open circle at height 4.

slides.title: Section 05 · AP practice
slides.html:
05Up next

AP-style multiple choice

slides.title: Question: jump discontinuity
slides.html:
Strategy

Mismatched one-sided limits ⇒ two-sided limit DNE.

Question PracticeTry it first

Work on paper, then check your reasoning.

At \(x=b\), \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to b^-} f(x)=3\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to b^+} f(x)=5\). Which is true?

Choose your answer

slides.title: Answer: jump
slides.html:
Answer ReviewCheck and correct

Compare your work with the model solution.

Correct Answer: C

✦
Your turnReveal only after you've written a full solution.

Solution:

Left limit 3, right limit 5 — two-sided limit does not exist.

slides.title: Question: read the piecewise graph
slides.html:
Strategy

The limit is the \(y\)-value approached from both sides — the open circle height.

Question PracticeTry it first

Work on paper, then check your reasoning.

Using the piecewise graph at \(x=2\) (open circle at \((2,3)\), filled dot at \((2,1.5)\)), what is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2} f(x)\)?

Choose your answer

slides.title: Answer: piecewise at 2
slides.html:
Answer ReviewCheck and correct

Compare your work with the model solution.

Correct Answer: B

✦
Your turnReveal only after you've written a full solution.

Solution:

Both sides approach \(y=3\); \(f(2)=1.5\) is separate.
